Modern.tagline: Wines from the edge of the appellation.
Modern.brandNameRationale: Verge is a real word for the edge of something — the road, the field, the season. It points to where the grapes are grown (the boundary between two soils, two climates, two appellations) without naming the place. Wine Co. is the plain category suffix. Reads in the lineage of modern wine brands like Day Wines, Broc Cellars, Field Recordings — evocative but never literal.
Modern.manifesto: Most modern wine brands sell either a place or a varietal. We made Verge because the actual interesting wines are made on the boundaries — the cold side of the hill, the last picking before the rain, the parcel that nobody planted on purpose. The brand is the edge, not the center. Each bottle is from a single parcel we lease at the verge of something larger.
Modern.industrySummary: DTC wine has matured around two camps: the heritage estate (Caymus, Silver Oak) and the natural-wine bottle-shop set (Maison Noir, Broc). The opening underneath is for a modern grower-producer brand that talks about specific parcels in plain language, ships direct, and looks more like a design studio than a cellar.
Modern.competitorLandscape: Day Wines (daywines.com) holds the modern grower-producer slot well. Broc Cellars (broccellars.com) plays the natural-wine peer. Field Recordings (fieldrecordingswine.com) sits in the editorial-modern middle. Caymus (caymus.com) is the heritage reference we are not. We sit closer to Day and Field Recordings, with a single-parcel framing per bottle.
Modern.positioningStatement: Verge Wine Co. is a modern grower-producer that releases small-lot wines from single parcels on the edge of their appellations.
Modern.positioningRationale: We compete on specificity. Each label names the parcel, the elevation, the soil, the year. The customer is buying a specific patch of ground in a specific year — not a brand and not a varietal.

Together the surnames read as an established vineyard partnership operating multiple estates — the kind of holding entity that supplies bulk programs and retail private label, not consumer-facing premium.
Corporate.manifesto: Heaton & Vail Vineyards is a vineyard ownership and wine production company operating across multiple AVAs and appellations. We grow grapes on owned and leased land, produce wine under contract for retail private label and restaurant programs, and operate two regional bottling facilities. The buyer is a retail wine buyer, a hospitality group, or a private-label client.

The opening is for a serious vineyard-and-production company with operational depth, transparent pricing, and the capacity to handle private-label and contract production for retailers and hospitality groups.

Creative.tagline: A wine brand for the second bottle.
Creative.brandNameRationale: Decant is the trade verb for pouring wine carefully into a serving vessel. The definite article + Co suffix follows the considered-creative trade-name school.
Creative.manifesto: Most wine brands sell the first sip. The reverent moment. The notes on the back of the label. We made Second Bottle because the truth about wine is that the second one is when things get interesting. The brand is for the dinner that runs long, the conversation that gets honest, the moment people stop pretending to know what tannin means.
Creative.industrySummary: Wine branding has been earnest, terroir-led, and slightly precious. There's room for a brand that's loud, character-driven, sticker-friendly, and serious about good wine without taking itself too seriously.
Creative.competitorLandscape: Black Lips Brewing isn't wine but does this voice. Big Bad Wines (bigbadwines.com) sits closer. Some Young Punks (someyoungpunks.com) holds the irreverent label position. We sit warmer and more retail-friendly than any of them.
Creative.positioningStatement: A wine brand for the dinner that runs long.

Creative.tagline: Wines that don't take themselves seriously.
Creative.brandNameRationale: Marigold is a real botanical name, warm and slightly sun-faded — the opposite of the somber heritage register most wine brands use. 'Wine Project' frames the brand as ongoing and experimental rather than canonical. The pairing belongs to the contemporary creative wine school (Field Recordings, Day Wines, Broc Cellars) without copying any of them.
Creative.manifesto: Most wine brands are trying to sound like a 17th-century estate even when the winemaker is 34 and learned in a garage. We started Marigold because the actual fun of making wine right now is unfussy — co-fermenting weird varieties, releasing pet-nats with cartoon labels, putting a sticker on a bottle and seeing what happens. The brand is a project. The labels change. The wine is honest about being made by humans in a warehouse last September.
Creative.industrySummary: Natural and low-intervention wine has matured into a fully developed market with its own canon. There is real space for a brand that takes the creative-led wine premise and pushes harder on illustration, voice, and label design — closer to a record label than a winery.
Creative.competitorLandscape: Broc Cellars (broccellars.com) is the closest creative peer. Maison Noir (mnwines.com) holds the irreverent slot. Field Recordings (fieldrecordingswine.com) sits in the editorial-creative middle. Las Jaras (lasjaras.com) plays in the celebrity-creative position. We sit alongside Broc and Maison Noir, with a slightly louder visual register.
Creative.positioningStatement: Marigold Wine Project is a creative-led wine label releasing small-lot experimental wines with illustrated labels and an irreverent voice.
Creative.positioningRationale: The brand competes on personality and design as much as on the wine itself. Each release has its own commissioned label illustration. The brand voice is closer to a fanzine than a tasting room.

Creative.mission: To restore late-harvest wines as a primary category rather than a curiosity.
Creative.vision: A brand whose late-harvest portfolio becomes the standard reference for serious dessert and sweet-wine drinkers.

Creative.brandNameRationale: The Late Harvest is the real winemaking trade term for grapes picked after the main harvest. Naming the brand after the category stakes a clear creative position. The definite article + Co suffix follows the considered-creative trade-name school.
Creative.manifesto: Most wine programs treat late-harvest wines as a side note. We started The Late Harvest Co because the actual most interesting wines are often the ones picked last — botrytized, late-harvest, ice wines. The category is the brand.
Creative.industrySummary: Late-harvest wines are under-represented in modern wine retail. There is real space for a creative-led brand specializing entirely in the category.
Creative.competitorLandscape: Royal Tokaji (royal-tokaji.com) plays the heritage late-harvest peer reference. Inniskillin Wines (inniskillin.com) holds the ice-wine peer slot. Sauternes producers play heritage references. We sit alongside Royal Tokaji with broader late-harvest coverage.
